work.name: BioFuse
work.place: Traverse City & Grand Rapids, MI · Boise, ID
work.lede: BioFuse runs IV therapy, weight loss and TRT clinics across four markets in Michigan and Idaho. Their business runs on appointments booked through their website, which is exactly what the previous agency never bothered to measure. They spent about $75,000 in twelve months and reported page views as results.
work.seoDescription: The previous agency spent $75,000 in a year without ever tracking a booking. In our first 103 days the account recorded 568 of them, at $42 each.

story.problem: BioFuse's business runs on appointments booked through their website. For ten of the previous agency's final twelve months, the account had no tracking on the booking flow at all. About $75,000 was spent in a year, and the monthly reports counted page views as conversions.
story.did: We rebuilt the account from twelve overlapping campaigns to eight with one purpose each, fenced the spend in with negative keyword lists, put end-to-end tracking on the booking flow, and separated the four markets so each clinic's spend is reported on its own.
story.happened: In the ten weeks the previous agency's tracking existed, it recorded 21 bookings against about $17,500 of spend, $846 for every appointment. In our first 103 days the same website recorded 568 bookings at $42 each.

statBand.l: Bookings recorded in our first 103 days
of the top search spend we inherited was buying nothing
statBand.sub: About $7,700 of the top $11,600 went to terms with zero bookings or leads. Now fenced off with negative keyword lists.

evidence.heading: Search terms nobody would ever buy on purpose
evidence.body: The previous agency let broad match run unattended. Single clicks the client paid for:

evidence.heading: Paying for a competitor’s supplement brand
evidence.body: “Nugenix” is an over-the-counter testosterone booster sold in drugstores, not a service BioFuse offers, and not a customer looking for a clinic. Across three variations of the term the account spent about $344 for 7 clicks and zero leads.

evidence.heading: Paying for a sports bar
evidence.body: The Traverse City campaign bought the term “game day traverse city”, a local sports bar, for about $293 across 9 clicks. It produced one recorded conversion, which under their tracking setup could have been a page view.

evidence.heading: Campaigns bidding against each other
evidence.body: The account had duplicate, overlapping campaigns for the same services in the same cities. The term “iv therapy near me” was bought by seven different campaign and ad group combinations at the same time, costing about $1,150 for 77 clicks, roughly $15 per click, in a market where we now buy clicks at $3.11. Their Demand Gen campaign spent about $1,100 and recorded zero conversions of any kind.

evidence.heading: They never measured a single booking
evidence.body: This is the one that mattered most, and it is not a subtlety; it is the basic job. BioFuse’s business runs on appointments booked through their website. For ten of their final twelve months, the account had no tracking on the booking flow at all. Not one completed booking was recorded. Every optimization decision made on that account for the better part of a year was made blind to the only outcome that pays the bills. What the monthly reports counted as “conversions” instead: 2,517 “Start Booking, page view” (someone landing on a page), 1,408 “Local actions, website visits” and 1,217 “Local actions, other engagements”. In October 2025 they promoted the page view to a primary conversion, which is what Google’s bidding then chased, so the budget was being steered toward people who opened a page and left. That month the account reported 323 conversions. 305 of them were page views. The reported cost per lead looked like $24. It was not a real number, and nothing in the report the client was sent would have told them that.
evidence.quote: They optimized an account for a business that books appointments online without ever measuring a booking.

evidence.heading: Results, first 103 days
evidence.body: Booking tracking existed for exactly ten weeks of the previous agency’s tenure, because they didn’t put any in place until April 2026. Here is everything their tracking ever recorded, against our first 103 days:

head: Previous agency (Apr 1 – Jun 10 2026, their only tracked period)
Lumin (Jun 11 – Sep 22 2026)

evidence.heading: Why we don’t use the headline conversion number
evidence.body: If you open this account today, Google will tell you it produced 1,726 conversions in July. It didn’t. The booking flow fires a conversion at each of five steps, so one person booking an appointment can register five times. We report the fifth one, the completed booking, and we’re fixing the counter. An agency that wanted a better-looking case study would have used the bigger number.

work.method: All figures come from BioFuse’s Google Ads account and can be verified in it; dollar figures are rounded. Cost per click and clicks per day cover Search campaigns only and are measured identically in both periods. “Bookings” counts completed appointments booked on the BioFuse website, measured by the same tracking in both periods. The previous agency put no booking tracking in place until April 2026, so their figures cover April 1 to June 10 2026, the only period in their tenure where bookings were recorded at all.

story.problem: Behnke had more freight than drivers. Loads were being turned away because nobody was available to haul them, and the work lost that way ran into the hundreds of thousands of dollars. Job boards were not producing CDL-A drivers fast enough to close the gap.
story.did: Behnke asked whether ads could reach CDL-A drivers directly. Then we ran Google Ads aimed at licensed drivers looking for work and sent them straight to it.
story.happened: Every open seat was filled. A little over a month after launch, Behnke paused the campaign because there was no one left to hire. The page stays live for the next round.

items.t: “I do not know what I do not know.”
items.d: That is fair, and it is exactly what the free plan is for. You get the findings in writing, in plain English, and you are free to hand them to someone else.

body: When the PTA opened Jog-A-Thon sponsorships, Lumin took one — the money goes to the programs below.

The QR code is the other half of it. A banner is only worth printing if the people reading it get something out of it, so this is the same offer we would make any business that called us cold: a written marketing plan for your business, free, and yours to keep.

faqs.q: What actually counts as a referral?
faqs.a: A named introduction to a real decision-maker: a warm email, a call, a form submission with their details. Not a list of leads, not a scraped spreadsheet. It is registered to you for 90 days from the day you make it.

faqs.q: When do I get paid?
faqs.a: 30 days after each of their invoices clears, then monthly for 12 months. Every payment comes with the invoice it was calculated from, so you can check the maths yourself.

faqs.q: What if they only buy a website and never come back?
faqs.a: Then you earn 10% of the build and hosting, and that is the end of it. One rate on everything is the whole point. There is nothing to read twice and nothing that pays out differently depending on which service they picked.

faqs.q: Do I have to be a client to refer someone?
faqs.a: No. Most of the best referrers are not clients. They are the accountant, the designer or the IT provider who gets asked the question. Clients get the one extra option: credit instead of cash, at 1.5× the value.

faqs.q: What happens to the person I send us?
faqs.a: They get the same free audit as anyone else: read-only access, findings they keep either way, and a person on the phone rather than a deck. Your name is attached to that introduction, so we treat it as yours to protect.

faqs.q: Is there a cap?
faqs.a: No cap, and no tier you have to hit before anything pays out. The first referral pays at the same rate as the tenth.

faqs.q: What if they were already talking to you?
faqs.a: We will tell you within one business day. If they have been in an active conversation with us in the last 90 days, it is not a referral, and you will hear that from us immediately rather than discovering it when nothing arrives.

faqs.q: I'm an attorney, or I work in healthcare. Can I take a percentage?
faqs.a: No, and we would rather say so up front. Percentage-of-revenue referral fees are restricted by state bar rules for attorneys and can implicate the federal Anti-Kickback Statute where healthcare providers are involved. Regulated referrers are offered a flat fee at fair market value, in a written agreement your compliance counsel signs off. Ask and we will send the paper.

faqs.q: Can my company be the referrer rather than me personally?
faqs.a: Yes, and for most people it should be. Payment goes wherever the W-9 says: your business, your LLC, or you.

referrals.headline: 10% of everything a business you refer pays us, for their first 12 months.

rules.t: Register it before we talk to them
rules.d: An introduction is yours from the day you make it, for 90 days. If they come to us cold first and you register them afterwards, it is not a referral, and we will tell you that on the day rather than at invoice time.

rules.t: Paid on money collected, never on money invoiced
rules.d: If a client never pays, there is nothing to share. We are not going to pay you for revenue we did not receive, and you would not want us to fund it out of the next one.

Commission is on what the client pays GoLumin. Media budget passes straight through to Google, Meta and Microsoft. We do not mark it up and we do not pay commission on it. A $40,000 ad budget is not $4,000 to you, and any programme that says otherwise is lying to one of you.
The 10% runs for 12 months from their first paid invoice. If they leave in month four, you keep everything paid to that point and the rest simply stops. Nothing is clawed back.

ACH in US dollars, or, if you are a client, 1.5× the cash value as credit against your own invoices. The credit is worth more; the cash is yours to spend. Over $600 in a year we will need a W-9 and will issue a 1099-NEC.
You cannot refer a business you own or control, and you cannot bid on GoLumin's brand terms or dress up as us to collect. This is an introduction programme between people, not an affiliate link.
After the introduction you are out of the loop unless you want to be in it. You will not be forwarded scoping threads, and we will not use you to chase an invoice.

steps.d: Use the form, forward an email, or just copy us in. We need the business name and a way to reach someone who can make a decision. That registers it to you for 90 days.

Same free audit everyone gets: read-only access, real findings, a person walking them through it. They keep the findings whether or not they hire us. No hard sell, because your name is on this introduction.
You hear which, from us, either way. If they were already in our pipeline we tell you within a day rather than letting you wonder.
10% of every invoice they pay, for 12 months, sent 30 days after their money clears. Monthly, by ACH, with the invoice it came from attached.

who.t: Clients we've already earned it from
who.d: You have seen the work, you know what we bill, and you are the referral a prospect actually believes. Take cash, or take it as credit on your own invoice at 1.5×.
who.line: You already do this for free

who.d: You build beautiful sites and have no interest in running someone's Google Ads, chasing their Maps listing or answering a call about a broken form at 9pm. Hand that part over and keep the client relationship.
who.line: Keep the design work, hand off the rest

who.d: You are already the person a local business calls when something digital breaks, which means you are asked about the website constantly. It is not your line of work, but the referral is worth real money.
You see the marketing line on the P&L and you know exactly which clients are lighting money on fire with an agency that cannot show them a lead. You are the most credible referrer on this list.
who.line: You can see the wasted spend

who.d: An SEO shop with no paid arm. A paid shop that will not touch a CMS. A branding studio that does not build. Send the part you do not want; we do not go after the part you do.
who.line: Send the half you don't want

who.d: You have a membership that all needs the same three things and keeps asking you who to use. A standing arrangement with terms you can publish to members is a straightforward one to set up.
who.line: Your members keep asking who to use

process.d: The form below, or an email. Tell us what you have built or run. A link beats a résumé; a real example beats both.
45 minutes with a person who does the work, not a recruiter. What you would own, what we are actually like, and your questions.
A paid exercise or a working session on an actual problem — an account, a codebase, a market. No take-home that takes your weekend.
An answer either way, with a reason. Compensation is discussed openly at this point, against what you would own.

roles.title: Full-stack engineer
roles.promise: Build the two platforms the whole agency runs on.
roles.lede: We built our own ads platform and our own CMS, and every client engagement runs through them. You would work across both: the agent layer that drafts the work, the approval gates that stop anything shipping on its own, and the ad-platform and publishing integrations underneath.
owns: Features across Lumin Ads and Lumin CMS, end to end — schema, jobs, API, UI
The agent layer: tool definitions, prompt templates, evals, budgets and run lifecycle
The approval gates and guardrails — the code that makes it impossible to overspend
Integrations with Google Ads, Meta, Microsoft Advertising, ChatGPT Ads and Search Console
Making the thing fast and keeping it boring to operate

stack.d: Both products. Conventional Rails, no microservices, no clever architecture for its own sake.
Server-driven routing, React views. The CMS is TypeScript with the React compiler on; the ads app is still JavaScript.
CSS-first config, OKLCH token layer, shadcn primitives aliased onto our own tokens. Per-tenant branding flows through CSS custom properties.
activerecord-tenanted. Each client's data is a separate file, not a WHERE clause. No Postgres, and we are not looking to add it.
All async work, caching and websockets on the database. No Redis and no Sidekiq anywhere.

stack.t: RubyLLM, plus a Claude Code harness
stack.d: Inference goes through one door — a single service class, enforced by a test that fails the build if anyone calls around it. A second executor runs Claude Code on worker boxes over MCP.
Self-hosted on our own boxes, deployed with Kamal. No Heroku, no Vercel, no managed platform between you and the machine.
Including tests that assert the shape of the codebase, not just its behaviour — that every agent template is valid, that inference has one door.

need: Real production Rails experience — you have owned a schema, a background job system and a deploy
Comfortable in React, or clearly able to get there fast
You write tests because you want the thing to keep working, not because someone asked
You can read a codebase you did not write and change it without breaking it
You explain a technical trade-off in plain language to someone non-technical
bonus: You have worked with an ad platform API — Google Ads, Meta Marketing, or similar
You have shipped something with an LLM in the loop and learned where it fails
You have run your own infrastructure and have opinions about it
You have built multi-tenant software and know where the sharp edges are
roles.honest: Both codebases are young and moving. The ads app is mid-migration from ERB to Inertia. The CMS has RSpec but no continuous integration yet, and Capybara installed with no browser specs written. None of that is hidden from you on day one — and all of it is work somebody gets to own.
roles.growth: There is no engineering layer above you to wait behind. The first engineer here shapes how we build, and grows into leading the product engineering team as it grows under them.

roles.title: Local SEO + AI search lead
roles.promise: Own whether our clients get found — on maps, in search results, and in AI answers.
roles.lede: Search split in two. People still type into Google, and they also ask an assistant for a plumber, a lawyer, a storage unit near them. Both answers come from the same raw material, and you own it: the pages, the entities, the citations and the consistency across every market a client serves.
owns: Local and AI search visibility for a book of local and multi-location clients
Location and service page systems — hundreds of pages per client, each one genuinely different
Business detail consistency across the site, listings and structured data
Directing the CMS agent crew: freshness, internal linking, metadata, schema, content gaps, cannibalisation
Being the named editor who approves what an agent drafted before it publishes

stack.d: Our own system. Pages, locations, collections and revisions in one place, with a page live under a minute after you approve it.

Eight of them, each with one job and a schedule: technical SEO, metadata, schema markup, internal linking, content freshness, content gaps, cannibalisation, alt text. They research and draft. You decide.
Wired into the CMS, so query and page data sits next to the thing you would change.
One client has 343 town pages and 272 zip-code pages. You work at that scale without letting the pages turn into duplicates.
Broken link scans, content freshness reports, asset usage audits and sitemap pings run on their own and surface what needs a human.

need: You have moved local search results for real businesses and can talk through how
You understand local search as a system — pages, listings, entities, reviews, consistency — not a checklist
You can write, and you can judge whether something an agent drafted is actually true
You are honest about what is measurable and what is not, especially with AI search
You are comfortable being the person whose name is on the approval
bonus: You have worked with a headless CMS or structured content model
Technical enough to read a sitemap, a schema blob and a server log without help
You have already been experimenting with how assistants cite sources
roles.honest: AI search visibility is a young discipline full of people selling certainty they do not have. We would rather you say what is controllable and what is not. That is a harder job and a more durable one.
roles.growth: This is the first dedicated search hire. It becomes the head of the search practice — defining the process, then hiring and leading the people who run it.

roles.title: Google Ads manager
roles.promise: Run a book of Google and Microsoft accounts toward qualified leads, not cheap clicks.
roles.lede: Agents work the accounts around the clock — mining search terms, pacing budget, auditing conversion tracking, rewriting tired copy. Every change they want to make waits in a queue for a person. You are that person, and you are accountable for what the spend actually produced.
owns: A book of Google Ads and Microsoft Advertising accounts, and what they deliver
The approvals queue for those accounts — approving, rejecting, and saying why
Spend caps, pacing and the conversion tracking that everything else depends on
Closing the loop: sold and lost lead outcomes fed back as offline conversions
The client relationship on media — you talk to them, not through an account manager

stack.d: Our own platform. Every channel in one place, one approvals queue, and a record of every change with the evidence attached.
Waste cutter, search term harvest, budget pacing, creative refresh, growth research. Each proposes with the money at stake attached. None can apply anything.
Spend caps enforced at the apply gate, in code. A proposal over the cap is blocked even if you approve it. You set the caps with the client.
Google Tag Manager integration, call tracking, customer match, and offline conversion upload — so bidding optimises toward customers.
Run as part of the same portfolio rather than an afterthought nobody logs into.

need: You have managed Google Ads spend you were genuinely accountable for
You can audit a conversion tracking setup and find the thing that is silently broken
You think in qualified leads and cost per sale, not clicks and impressions
You can reject a confident recommendation when the evidence does not hold up
You can explain to a client why you did something, in their language
bonus: Local business or lead-gen experience specifically — legal, medical, home services or similar
You have worked with offline conversion imports and know why they matter
Google Ads scripts, the API, or any history of automating your own work
roles.honest: The agents will find things faster than you would alone, and they will also be confidently wrong sometimes. The job is judgement at volume. If you want to hand-build every campaign yourself, you would be bored here.
roles.growth: Grows into leading the paid media practice across every channel — setting how accounts are run, and hiring the team that runs them.

roles.title: Meta Ads manager
roles.promise: Own paid social as part of one portfolio, not a silo with its own scoreboard.
roles.lede: Meta is where the demand that has not started searching yet lives. You own it for a book of clients — creative strategy, audience structure, lead quality — inside the same approvals queue and the same feedback loop as everything else we run.
owns: A book of Meta accounts and what they produce in qualified leads
Creative strategy and the testing cadence behind it
Lead ad quality — the difference between a form fill and someone who answers the phone
Approving or rejecting what the agents propose on your accounts
Working with the Google Ads manager as one portfolio, sized against each other

stack.d: Meta sits in the same platform, the same approvals queue and the same reporting as search. One place, one record.
They surface fatigue and draft variants. You own the brief, the judgement and the brand.
Sold and lost go back to Meta as offline conversions, so optimisation learns what a customer looks like instead of what a form fill looks like.
Every account stays in the client's name. You work inside their asset, with access they can revoke.

need: You have run Meta lead generation for local businesses and know how bad a cheap lead can be
You have a real point of view on creative — what to test, and how to tell what won
You are comfortable with audience structure, exclusions and the current state of tracking
You can write a brief someone else could execute
You care what happened after the lead came in
bonus: You can produce or direct creative yourself
You have worked with the Conversions API or offline event uploads
Any experience running paid social alongside search rather than separately
roles.honest: Paid social in a lead-gen business is judged on lead quality, and lead quality data is always messier than the dashboard suggests. We would rather argue about the messy number than celebrate the clean one.
roles.growth: Grows into owning paid social across the book, and into the paid media leadership the practice will need as it scales.

values.d: Three services, one team, one record. Nobody here gets to optimise their own number at another person's expense — the whole point of the company is that the handoffs do not leak.
Nobody will hand you a ticket queue. You will find the problem, write up what you would do, and go. Asking permission for everything is slower than we can afford.

Agents propose, a named person approves, the software enforces the limits. That only works if the person signing is genuinely careful. Accuracy, follow-through, and saying no to a plausible-looking bad idea.

Early team, flat structure, no layer to wait behind. The people who join now define how their function works and then lead it. Compensation is expected to move with that, and we would rather talk about it honestly than post a band we would outgrow.
